sentences.text: Here is a synthetic task.
How many rows in orders dot C S V have a null customer I D?
The correct answer is seven.
A scripted probe answers seventeen.
The naive grader marks it correct, because the digit seven appears somewhere in the answer.
Every score built on that grader inherits the error.
So before trusting a benchmark score, it's worth testing the grader.
Grader Audit tests graders without running any model.
It feeds them scripted probes: fixed outputs with a known label, should pass or should fail.
A grader can be wrong in three ways.
A false positive passes an output that should fail.
A false negative fails an output that should pass.
A flaky verdict changes between repeated runs of the same input.
This is an independent prototype using synthetic tasks and scripted probes.
It does not audit HUD's actual benchmarks.
The bench has twelve synthetic data engineering tasks: four questions, five tables, and three pipeline run records to update.
Each task gets eight probes, from the exact gold output to traps and partly wrong answers.
Labels depend on the task.
Shuffled rows are fine, except in a top five ranking, where order is the answer.
That makes ninety-six cases.
Forty-seven should pass, and forty-nine should fail.
One command runs everything: Python, dash m, audit dot serve.
It generates the data, runs both graders five times per case, and serves this page.
The five runs are combined by majority vote into one verdict per case, and that verdict is what gets counted.
The naive graders passed twenty of forty-nine should-fail cases, and failed fourteen of forty-seven should-pass cases.
Six of ninety-six were flaky.
The hardened graders made no errors, on these ninety-six synthetic cases only.
The error-count heatmap shows wrong verdicts for each probe and grader.
Click a cell to list its cases.
Here's the substring trap on the naive grader.
Case A1 shows the instruction, the probe's seventeen, and the gold seven.
The label says should fail.
The naive grader passed it, because the output contains seven.
The hardened grader failed it: numeric mismatch.
In table case T four, one regional total is off by a dollar.
The naive check sees the right header and row count, and passes.
The diff shows the changed row.
Task A2 asks for the total of completed orders.
The probe writes the gold amount with a dollar sign and a thousands comma.
The value is unchanged, so it should pass.
The naive substring check fails it.
The hardened exact check fails too, so it asks the judge.
In this run, that's the deterministic mock judge, not a model.
It extracts one number and compares within half a cent.
Order is different.
In the top five table, the hardened grader correctly fails shuffled rows.
Task S one has a planted naive check: the finish time must be under three hundred seconds old.
Each of the five runs gets a simulated clock, set by its seed.
Two of the five delays cross the limit, so the verdicts read: fail, pass, fail, pass, pass.
The audit flags six flaky cases, all on this grader.
Two caveats.
The clock variation is controlled, so detection works by construction.
And the majority vote hides some errors: this correct output failed two of five runs, but isn't counted as a false negative.

scenes.title: How the code produces the report

sentences.text: Here's how one case reaches the screen.
Build tasks creates task A1 and its gold answer.
Build probes creates the seventeen, labeled should fail.
Generate writes both to disk.
Run audit loads every case, and grade k calls each grader five times with a seeded context.
The majority verdict is tagged a false positive, counted in the summary and heatmap, and written to results dot json and the report.
FastAPI serves it to this page.
The hardened graders parse each output by its declared type, with float tolerance, null markers, date formats, and row order only when the task requires it.
State checks compare every field, not just a done flag.
For answers, the exact check runs first, and the judge is called only when it fails.
That happened twenty-six times here, all with the mock judge.
A real model judge is supported, but wasn't run.
And since the mock's rules were written alongside these probes, its agreement is not independent validation.
The evidence.
One hundred fifty-two tests pass: one hundred thirty-nine unit, thirteen integration.
They include every hardened grader against all eight probes.
A mutation test swaps an equality check for a substring check in the hardened answer grader, and the audit reports a false positive on the A1 trap.
So the harness measures all three error types against known labels, and separates the two graders on these ninety-six synthetic cases.
It doesn't show the hardened graders are correct in general.
They were written knowing these probe types.
Nor does it cover real environments, or a real model judge.
Future work: human-reviewed, model-generated adversarial probes, and adapters for real environments.
